title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Introduction
content: Numerous instruments are utilized during oral surgical procedures, each having a specific role (see Image. An Oral Surgery Instruments Kit). Dental practitioners should be able to select appropriate instruments in given situations, preventing iatrogenic damage and traumatic procedures and thus increasing patient safety. This topic introduces several commonly used instruments during various oral surgical procedures, but does not provide an exhaustive list.

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Examination Kit
content: A clinical examination must be performed before performing any oral surgical procedure. A standard kit includes a dental mouth mirror, probe, and tweezers. These instruments can be combined within separate disposable kits or included within a standard oral surgery procedure kit. [1] After administering local anesthesia, its efficacy can be tested using objective signs, which can put the patient at ease before initiating the surgical procedure. This includes applying firm pressure with a probe adjacent to the tooth to be extracted, down the periodontal ligament, to prevent pain. [2]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Local Anesthetic Delivery Systems
content: Local anesthesia is essential in dentistry to eliminate pain and anxiety during dental procedures. Conventional syringes and needles are commonly used with a handle to administer local anesthesia. In the 1990s, computer-assisted systems were developed to provide predictable pulpal anesthesia, lowering the overall dose delivered and, in turn, reducing the risk of collateral anesthesia. [3] Additionally, to minimize the risk of administering anesthesia directly into a blood vessel, self-aspirating syringes are frequently used. [4] Needles and sharp instruments can pose a risk of needle-stick injury to the operator. Modern safety syringes minimize this risk by using a sheath that, when activated, locks over the needle to prevent accidental injury. [5]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Periotomes and Luxators
content: These fine instruments are used to shear the periodontal ligament and act as a wedge to expand the socket. [6] [7] These are inserted between the tooth and socket and moved around the tooth to create space for the use of elevators and forceps while applying gentle pressure apically. [8] [9] A more atraumatic technique can be achieved by carefully widening a socket and making space for appropriate instruments, facilitating a good surface for implant placement through bone preservation. [10] When the root apex fractures within the socket, a root pick elevator can help luxate the apical tip. When the surgeon struggles to identify a definitive application point, apical root tip bone removal may be required to improve access. These fine instruments have a posterior curve of the working end, allowing for successful application and luxation. [9]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Elevators
content: A range of dental elevators is available to mobilize teeth by applying controlled forces that sever the periodontal ligament and gradually expand the socket. These instruments function through leverage, but excessive force risks damaging adjacent structures and producing iatrogenic injuries such as alveolar fractures. [9] The elevators most frequently used in practice include Coupland, Warwick-James, and Cryer designs. [8] [11] Each can be positioned between the crestal bone and the tooth or root surface, relying on the mechanical principles of a lever, wedge, and wheel to elevate and dislodge the tooth. [7] [12]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Elevators
content: Cryer elevators feature a sharp point designed to impart rotational forces. They are particularly effective for removing the mesial or distal roots of mandibular molars when engaged in the interseptal bone. [8] Warwick-James elevators are supplied as a set of 3—straight, curved left, and curved right—to suit different access needs. [11] Coupland elevators typically come in 3 progressively larger sizes, allowing the clinician to increase elevation force as additional space is created. [9]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Dental Extraction Forceps
content: Dental extraction forceps are used to remove teeth from their sockets and grip onto either the crown or the root surface. They usually act as levers; however, some also create a wedge effect. [7] They are positioned as apically as possible, and rotational, buccolingual, or a combination of these movements are applied to remove the teeth. Various forceps are available depending on whether the tooth is in the maxillary or mandibular arch, and whether it is a molar, premolar, or anterior tooth. Maxillary root forceps are suitable for use with any maxillary root, and similarly, mandibular root forceps can be applied to any mandibular root. Cowhorn forceps can be used for either the maxillary molar or mandibular molar teeth and are designed so that their beak is seated into the furcation of molar teeth. Applying pressure then luxates the tooth coronally, allowing for simple delivery. They can sometimes also be used to section molar teeth, facilitating individual root delivery. Care should be taken to avoid fracturing the buccal plate from excessive force. [8]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Mouth Props
content: Mouth props or bite blocks are placed in the mouth to hold the teeth apart. Certain oral surgical procedures require patients to keep their mouths open for extended periods. The use of mouth props allows patients to bite on these, so they do not have to hold their mouths open for the duration of the procedure. [12] Gutters are present within the top and bottom of the prop, in which the teeth or alveolar ridge sit. They are usually made of rubber and have an attached chain outside the mouth to make the prop easy to retrieve. [13] In patients with a hyperactive gag reflex, the insertion of a mouth prop can trigger their response, and they may be unable to tolerate it during the procedure. [14] Mouth props come in various sizes, so clinical judgment should be used to determine the most appropriate option.

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Retractors
content: These instruments retract soft tissue structures, such as raised flaps. [8] Retraction is essential for handling soft tissues during the surgical procedure to perform it optimally. Retractors commonly used include Lack, Laster, Bowdley Henry rake, Minnesota, Austin, and Kilner retractors, which can be used in various clinical situations. [15] The Lack tongue retractor helps to stabilize the tongue, improving visualization. [16] The Laster retractor can be useful when extracting upper third molars to retract the soft tissues and direct light posteriorly towards the maxillary tuberosity region. [15] Bowdler Henry rakes, Minnesota retractors, or Austin retractors are often used during surgical extractions to retract the buccal mucoperiosteal flap, improving visibility and access while preventing flap damage. [17] The Kilner cheek retractor is routinely used to retract the cheeks or the lips, improving access to the surgical field within the oral cavity. [18]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Scalpel Handle and Blade
content: A scalpel is required for certain oral surgical procedures, such as raising a mucoperiosteal flap; commonly, a 15-blade is used in a Bard Parker Handle. [8] [12] A scalpel can also be used to carry out incisional and excisional intra-oral biopsies. Usually, the inferior incision is made first so as not to obscure vision due to the hemorrhage. Tissue forceps are then used to lift and transfer the sample into a suitable medium. [19] A scalpel is the instrument of choice for incision and intra-oral and extra-oral abscess drainage. [20] [21]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Periosteal Elevators
content: When raising a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap, the mucosa and periosteum must be cleanly reflected together completely down to the bone to limit trauma to the underlying tissues and improve the healing process when the flap is repositioned. This is usually performed with a pushing motion using a periosteal elevator, such as a Howarth periosteal elevator. Sometimes periosteal elevators are used to retract the flap, for example, to protect the lingual nerve. [12] [22] The Ward periosteal elevator has a spoon-shaped end, which helps scoop up and reflect mucoperiosteal flaps. [23] Similarly, a Mitchell trimmer can be used as an elevator because it has a spoon-shaped end. The curvature of these 2 instruments is beneficial during cyst enucleation within bony structures, enabling the surgeon to carefully separate the cyst lining from the underlying bone and prevent cyst rupture, which can then be sent for histopathological assessment completely intact. [24]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Surgical Straight Handpiece
content: A surgical straight handpiece that does not expel air into the surgical site can be used to section teeth and remove bone when necessary. It is prudent to use a handpiece that does not expel air to avoid surgical emphysema, and it must be cooled with sterile saline. [8] [12] [25] Most commonly, round burs are used to remove the alveolar bone. During tooth removal, surgeons may use a fissure bur to section the crown and root. [26] [27] Fissure burs are also used for coronectomy procedures, which involve removing the crown of the tooth and reducing the remaining roots 3mm below the crest of the buccal and lingual plates. [28] Bone rongeurs are instruments used to aid bone removal. They can remove bony prominences or irregular ridges, which can be smoothed with a bone file, thereby improving healing. [8]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Suction
content: Good suction is necessary to maintain a clear field for optimal surgical site visualization and to prevent patient ingestion or aspiration. [29] [30] Many suction tips exist, with Frazier and Yankaeur most commonly used in oral surgical procedures. Yankauer suction is usually plastic tubing, while Frazier suction is usually a metal suction tip. [29] Frazier suction is particularly useful during surgical procedures such as surgical tooth extractions. It has a bend in the shaft, making it easier to access deeper structures, including the apical area of extraction sockets. The hole where it is held can be occluded with a finger to provide stronger suction when needed; lighter suction is usually required on soft tissues than on hard tissues. [30]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Sutures
content: Various suture materials can be utilized depending on the procedure and clinician preference. They can be grouped into resorbable or non-resorbable. Resorbable sutures include those made from polygalactic, polydioxanone, and polyglycolic acid. Nonresorbable sutures include those made from silk, polyamides, and polyesters. [31] Resorbable sutures are most commonly used for oral surgical procedures. [12] Suture needles are available in different shapes, sizes, and alloys depending on the size and depth of the closed tissue. [32] The suture needle is held in a suture holder, which aids in passing the needle through soft tissues; suture holders often lock to keep the needle secure. [32] The suture holder should grasp the needle approximately one-third from the swage to the tip to prevent needle fracture, bending, and twisting. [32]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Function -- Scissors
content: Various scissors are available in different shapes and sizes for cutting soft tissues, sutures, oxidized resorbable cellulose, and dissected tissues. [12] Different scissors have different uses; for example, curved McIndoe scissors are preferred for dissection and tissue cutting. [33] Mayo scissors can have curved or straight blades and are often used for cutting tissues and sutures. [34]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Clinical Significance
content: The instruments reviewed are fundamental to many oral surgical procedures. As such, it is necessary to be aware of their existence, appreciate the clinical situations they are used in, and understand how they can be applied. This knowledge facilitates their safe use, as improper instrumentation, in combination with uncontrolled excessive force, can have detrimental effects, such as iatrogenic mandibular fractures. [35] This reading should be supplemented with practical experience, as a particular method for a procedure does not always work in another clinician's hands. Several different instruments can often be used in the same clinical scenario, and clinicians develop a preference.

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The World Health Organisation launched the Surgical Safety Checklist in 2009, allowing different treatment stages to be checked before commencing a procedure. This can be modified for oral surgical procedures to minimize the risk of adverse outcomes. [36] The entire dental team involved in the surgery must conduct the pre-operative checks, and patient involvement is encouraged. Pauses in the form of verbal checks may be used before an invasive procedure, such as administering local anesthesia, or before using an oral surgical instrument, such as an elevator or forceps. [37] All team members involved in oral surgical procedures must be aware of the available instruments, prepare the surgical kits appropriately, and request and use the specific instruments required.

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Dental nurses often undertake decontamination tasks when there is no dedicated staff member for cleaning and sterilizing instruments. All dental care professionals must understand and be trained in cross-infection control, which is essential in dentistry given the exposure-prone nature of many procedures. [37] Following thorough decontamination protocols ensures instruments are safe for patient use. The dental practitioner uses sharp instruments, such as a scalpel and a local anesthetic needle, during oral surgical procedures. It is therefore essential that, at the end of the surgery, the dentist takes responsibility for disposing of these sharp instruments carefully. Proper sharps management reduces the risk of sharps injuries and contact with potentially infectious material to the person who clears the instrument tray. [38]

title: Oral Surgery, Instruments -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Monitoring
content: Four-handed dentistry can be utilized to maximize efficiency during oral surgical procedures. The dental nurse recognizes the required instrument next or is instructed by the dental practitioner, and then provides it to them. [39] A sound understanding of oral surgical instruments is imperative, as there are often many instruments on the tray, and delays in treatment can result if the assistant cannot identify each instrument and pass it to the operator in a timely manner. Additionally, the wider team must know how to use various instruments to identify faulty pieces and report and replace them.
